newsitem.title: USA: Dollar climbs amid talk of higher interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar climbs amid talk of higher interest rates.

text.p: The dollar rose against most currencies, boosted by mounting expectations for higher U.S. interest rates and continuing speculation that Europe's efforts to forge a single currency will be delayed.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told reporters that the stumbling German economy had prevented interest rate hikes in Germany, but added that the weak German mark and the likelihood of higher U.S. interest rates ruled out a cut in German rates.

"The prospect of even more favourable interest rate differentials between the U.S. and Germany is very supportive for the dollar," said Seth Garrett, a director of foreign exchange at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Higher domestic interest rates make returns on U.S. investments more attractive, boosting demand for dollars.

Many economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise its short-term interest rate targets in the Spring, a view that gained supporters after Chairman Alan Greenspan last Wednesday told a Senate committee the central bank might tighten credit even before it saw rising inflation.
Recent data show solid economic expansion in the United States, including a government report on Monday showing steady growth in consumer spending.
Another report from the National Association of Purchasing Management showed surprising strength and hints of inflation in the manufacturing sector.
Welteke also said further appreciation of the dollar versus the mark was undesirable and that a delay in the proposed European economic and monetary union (EMU) would boost the mark strongly.
Welteke's first comment hurt the dollar, but investors later pushed the dollar higher against the mark.
"Welteke made a couple of comments, the first of which was bullish for the mark and the second seemed to offset it," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Another Bundesbank council member, Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, was quoted in the newspaper Berliner Zeitung saying he was not sure the proposed European economic and monetary union would begin in 1999 as scheduled.

While those comments triggered sales of Spanish pesetas and Italian lire for marks, investors sold the German unit against the dollar and the Swiss franc, which are seen as safe havens from EMU uncertainty.
"It's questionable whether people will actually go back into marks or would the dollar be a smarter place to go," Garrett said.
The dollar climbed to 1.6970 marks from 1.6894 late Friday, but ended flat at 1.4775 Swiss francs. The U.S. unit also advanced to 121.24 Japanese yen from 120.17.
The British pound fell to $1.6178 from $1.6285. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3675 from C$1.3682.
Traders in Europe said the central banks in Italy and Spain had entered the foreign exchange markets to sell marks in an effort to prop up their currencies.
